title: [ISSUE] ztw_helpers.validate_and_convert_country_code silently returns the first of several ambiguous fuzzy matches ("Korea" -> COUNTRY_KP)

blocks.heading: [ISSUE] ztw_helpers.validate_and_convert_country_code silently returns the first of several ambiguous fuzzy matches ("Korea" -> COUNTRY_KP)

blocks.text: **Title:** `[ISSUE] ztw_helpers.validate_and_convert_country_code silently returns the first of several ambiguous fuzzy matches ("Korea" -> COUNTRY_KP)`
**Description**

`validate_and_convert_country_code()` resolves its input through a chain of exact `pycountry` getters and then falls back to `pycountry.countries.search_fuzzy()`. When the fuzzy search returns **several** candidates, the helper takes `countries[0]` and returns it as if it were an unambiguous answer — no error, no warning, no indication that a choice was made (`src/zscaler_mcp/common/ztw_helpers.py:56-63` on master `809f68d`):

The five exact getters above it (`ztw_helpers.py:48-54`) are all single-answer lookups, so `countries[0]` is only ever reached on the fuzzy path — i.e. exactly the path where more than one answer is possible.

The clearest case is the word `Korea`, which matches both `KP` and `KR` and resolves to `KP`. Because the return value is a valid, well-formed `COUNTRY_XX` string, it carries no confidence signal: neither the caller nor a later reviewer can tell "matched exactly" from "picked one of several".

This is not limited to one input. Sweeping every word of length >= 4 that appears in a `pycountry` country name, and keeping only the words that miss all five exact getters *and* yield more than one fuzzy candidate, gives **66 distinct inputs** that resolve to a silently chosen country:

| input | returned | other candidates that also matched | |---|---|---| | `KOREA` | `COUNTRY_KP` | `KR` | | `VIRGIN ISLANDS` | `COUNTRY_VG` | `VI`, `US` | | `KINGDOM` | `COUNTRY_BE` | `BH`, `BT`, `DK`, … | | `HONG` | `COUNTRY_HK` | `CN`, `LA`, `TH` | | `FEDERATION` | `COUNTRY_RU` | `CH` | | `CENTRAL` | `COUNTRY_BW` | `FJ`, `GH`, `PG` | | `ISLAMIC` | `COUNTRY_AF` | `MR`, `PK`, `IR` |
The docstring (`ztw_helpers.py:25-27`) documents the resolution order but not the tie-break:

blocks.code:
Resolution order (first match wins): existing ``COUNTRY_XX`` validation →
alpha-2 → alpha-3 → name → common name → official name → fuzzy search.
Raises ``ValueError`` if nothing matches.

blocks.text: "first match wins" reads as *first stage* wins, not *first of several candidates within the fuzzy stage* wins.
Two properties make this worth fixing rather than documenting:

blocks.item: **The wrong answer is indistinguishable from the right one.** A well-formed `COUNTRY_XX`

blocks.text: string looks identical either way, and the only caller (`ztw_create_ip_destination_group`, via `validate_and_convert_country_codes` at `src/zscaler_mcp/tools/ztw/ip_destination_groups.py:157`) persists it and reports success. The discrepancy is visible only if someone reads the group back and re-checks each code by hand.

blocks.item: **The tie-break is not stable across versions.** `search_fuzzy()` ordering is a `pycountry`

blocks.text: implementation detail, and the declared constraint is `pycountry>=24.0.0` (`pyproject.toml:58`) — an unpinned lower bound. The same input can resolve to a different country after an unrelated dependency bump, with no change in this repository.

Note that `pycountry`'s exact getters are case-insensitive, so the `.strip().upper()` at `ztw_helpers.py:39` does **not** push full country names into the fuzzy path — `"Canada"` and `"CANADA"` both resolve exactly via `name`. Only genuinely partial or genuinely ambiguous input reaches the fallback, which is why the inputs that reach it are precisely the risky ones.
Found by reading the helper source, then reproduced locally.
**Reproduction**
No credentials or network access needed — the helper is pure.

blocks.code:
# repro.py
import pycountry
from zscaler_mcp.common.ztw_helpers import validate_and_convert_country_code as conv

for probe in ("Korea", "Virgin Islands"):
    candidates = [(c.alpha_2, c.name) for c in pycountry.countries.search_fuzzy(probe)]
    print(f"{probe!r} -> {conv(probe)}   candidates={candidates}")

blocks.text: **Expected behavior**

An input that matches more than one country is rejected with an error naming the alternatives, so the caller can retry with an unambiguous alpha-2 code — the same contract the sibling helper `normalize_iso_country_code()` (`src/zscaler_mcp/common/zpa_helpers.py:37-51`) already enforces for App Connector / Service Edge groups.
**Actual behavior**

blocks.code:
$ python repro.py
'Korea' -> COUNTRY_KP   candidates=[('KP', "Korea, Democratic People's Republic of"), ('KR', 'Korea, Republic of')]
'Virgin Islands' -> COUNTRY_VG   candidates=[('VG', 'Virgin Islands, British'), ('VI', 'Virgin Islands, U.S.'), ('US', 'United States')]

blocks.text: Both are silent picks from a multi-candidate result. `Virgin Islands` is a three-way tie that even includes an unrelated country (`US`).
**Other Information**
Suggested direction — refuse to guess when the fuzzy stage is ambiguous, and name the alternatives:

This keeps every currently-working input working. The existing tests (`tests/test_ztw_shaping.py:21-30`) cover `"Canada"`, `"US"`, `"COUNTRY_GB"` and `"Notalandia"`, and none of them reach the changed branch: `"Canada"` hits the exact `name` getter, `"US"` hits `alpha_2`, `"COUNTRY_GB"` returns from the `COUNTRY_` prefix branch, and `"Notalandia"` makes `search_fuzzy` raise `LookupError` and falls through to the existing final `ValueError`.

`"US"` is worth calling out as evidence that the exact-getter chain is load-bearing: `search_fuzzy("US")` returns 57 candidates, but `alpha_2` claims it first, so it never reaches the fallback. The change would only affect inputs that already had no single answer.
Two smaller alternatives if raising is too strict:

blocks.item: Keep `countries[0]` but log a `WARNING` naming the candidates, so the choice is at least

blocks.text: auditable.

blocks.item: Prefer an exact case-insensitive `name` hit among the fuzzy candidates before falling back to

blocks.text: `[0]`, and raise only when that is still ambiguous.

Whichever you prefer, the property that matters is that a multi-candidate fuzzy result stops being reported as a definite answer. Happy to open a PR in any of these three shapes — the raise variant is a five-line diff plus one test.
